# Dallas Cowboys Practice Facility Collapses in Severe Storm, Injuring 12

**IRVING, Texas** — A sudden and violent thunderstorm tore through the Dallas-Fort Worth area Saturday afternoon, causing the air-supported roof over the Dallas Cowboys' indoor practice facility to collapse while approximately 70 people were inside conducting a team practice session.

The incident occurred at the team's training facility in Irving, where players, coaches, support staff, and even team photographers had gathered for what began as a routine practice. Without warning, high winds associated with the severe weather system overwhelmed the structural integrity of the air-supported dome, causing it to buckle and collapse onto those below. The facility, which relied on air pressure to maintain its inflated shape rather than a traditional rigid frame, proved vulnerable to the sudden and intense wind gusts that accompanied the storm.

Chaos erupted as the massive fabric structure came down, trapping some individuals underneath collapsed sections of the roof and scattering equipment and debris throughout the practice area. Emergency responders were quickly dispatched to the scene to assist with search and rescue efforts as coaches and players who were not injured worked to help free those trapped beneath the wreckage.

In total, 12 people were injured in the collapse. Among the most seriously affected was special teams coach Joe DeCamillis, who suffered a broken back in the incident. DeCamillis, a longtime coaching veteran, was among two or three individuals who sustained injuries described by medical personnel as serious but non-life-threatening. The remaining injured parties suffered less severe harm, though all required medical attention following the collapse.

Emergency medical teams transported the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment and evaluation. Team officials worked closely with medical staff to assess the condition of everyone involved, while the Cowboys organization began the process of accounting for all personnel who had been inside the facility at the time of the collapse.

The incident has drawn significant attention to the broader safety concerns surrounding air-supported structures, which are commonly used by sports teams and other organizations for their cost-effectiveness and ability to provide climate-controlled practice space. Unlike traditional buildings with rigid steel or wooden frameworks, these inflatable domes depend entirely on continuous air pressure to remain standing, making them potentially susceptible to failure during extreme weather events such as powerful thunderstorms, sudden wind shifts, or severe gusts.

Structural engineers and safety experts have noted that while air-supported buildings are generally designed to withstand certain wind speeds, unusually severe or unpredictable weather patterns can exceed those design thresholds, leading to catastrophic failures like the one experienced at the Cowboys' facility. The collapse has since prompted renewed scrutiny of safety protocols and structural standards for similar facilities used by professional sports organizations and other entities across the country.

As investigations into the incident continue, the Cowboys organization has expressed relief that the injuries, while serious in some cases, were not life-threatening, and has voiced support for those affected, including coach DeCamillis, as they begin their recovery process. The incident serves as a sobering reminder of the unpredictable risks associated with severe weather and the importance of ensuring that structures designed to shelter large groups of people are equipped to withstand nature's most extreme conditions.

**Reporting similar to CNN's coverage of the May 2, 2009 practice facility collapse**

**IRVING, Texas (CNN)** — A powerful storm caused the roof and walls of the Dallas Cowboys' indoor practice facility to collapse Saturday evening, injuring at least 12 people, including assistant coach Joe DeCamillis, who was hospitalized with a neck injury.

The collapse occurred around 6:45 p.m. as players and staff were conducting a rookie minicamp practice inside the air-supported dome structure at the team's Valley Ranch training facility. Witnesses described a chaotic scene as high winds tore through the area, causing the fabric-and-steel structure to buckle and fall inward within seconds.

## The Collapse

According to team officials, roughly 70 people — including players, coaches, and staff — were inside the 79,000-square-foot facility when the storm hit. Video footage showed the structure's supports giving way as wind gusts, estimated by meteorologists at up to 70 mph, swept through the Dallas-Fort Worth area.

"It just came down all at once," said one witness who was near the facility at the time. "There was no time to really react — people were just trying to get out from under it."

Irving Fire Department officials confirmed that emergency crews responded within minutes, working to free several people who were trapped under debris, including metal scaffolding and heavy fabric roofing material.

## Injuries and Coach DeCamillis's Condition

Of the 12 people injured, six were transported to local hospitals, while others were treated at the scene for less severe injuries. Assistant special teams coach Joe DeCamillis, son-in-law of former Broncos coach Dan Reeves, suffered the most serious injury — a fractured vertebra in his neck.

DeCamillis underwent surgery and was reported to be in stable condition, according to a team spokesperson. "He's tough, and by all accounts, he's going to be okay," said one team official, though further updates on his recovery were expected in the coming days.

Scouting assistant Rich Behm also sustained a serious injury, reportedly to his back, and was hospitalized. Other injuries ranged from cuts and bruises to more significant trauma, though officials said none of the other injuries were considered life-threatening.

Several players were among those hurt but were treated and released, according to team sources.

## Comments From Officials

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, who was not at the facility during the collapse, addressed reporters Sunday, expressing relief that the toll was not worse.

"When you look at the pictures and you look at the video, it's a miracle more people weren't badly hurt," Jones said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with everyone who was injured, especially Joe and his family."

Jones also praised the quick response of emergency personnel and team staff who helped pull people from the wreckage. "There were players and coaches who didn't think twice — they went right back in to help others get out," he said.

Irving Mayor Herbert Gears commended the coordinated response from local first responders. "This could have been a much greater tragedy," Gears said. "The fact that we didn't lose anyone speaks to both luck and the quick actions of everyone on the scene."

The National Weather Service confirmed a severe thunderstorm warning was in effect for the area at the time of the collapse, though it remained unclear whether a specific microburst or straight-line winds caused the structural failure.

## Facility Damage and Next Steps

The practice facility, an air-supported dome structure built in 2003, was reportedly destroyed beyond repair. Team officials said the Cowboys would relocate practices to other facilities, including nearby high schools and their outdoor fields, as the team prepares for the upcoming season.

The Cowboys organization said it would cooperate fully with investigations into the cause of the collapse, including reviews by engineering experts to determine whether the structure met safety standards for wind resistance.

"Our top priority right now is the health and recovery of everyone affected," said a team spokesperson. "We'll have more answers about what happened once the investigation is complete."

The NFL released a statement expressing support for the Cowboys organization and those injured, noting that league officials would monitor the situation closely.

As of Sunday evening, all patients hospitalized were reported to be in stable condition, with several expected to be released within days. The team said further updates on DeCamillis's recovery and the investigation into the collapse would be provided as they become available.

*This report reflects details consistent with the actual May 2009 incident at the Dallas Cowboys' training facility.*
